RESOLUTION RULE (different shape from the rejected fix). A dependency binds to **the commit of that dependency the candidate's own history contains** — resolved by asking Git, newest-first, whether any commit the dependency has ever handed off is an ancestor of this candidate. Not the dependency's current approval, not its landing commit, not its card digest. And the binding goes stale only when the dependency's standing approval **does not contain** the bound commit. Containment, not equality, is what operationalizes invariant 7.3.6's word *relevant*: a dependency that gained review-requested fixes on top has moved without superseding anything (the merge carries one version); only a rewrite leaves the bound commit outside what will land (the merge carries two).

1. src/domain/handoff.rs
   - `pub struct DependencyBinding { card_id: CardId, incorporated_sha: Option<String> }` — recorded, `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`.
   - `pub struct DependencyStanding { card_id, approved_candidate_sha: Option<String>, approval_contains_binding: bool }` — resolved live; the ancestry bit is filled by the command layer because a record cannot carry an ancestry fact about a commit that did not exist when it was written.
   - `pub const DEPENDENCIES_NOT_CHECKED: &[DependencyStanding] = &[]`.
   - `pub(crate) fn dependency_staleness(subject, bindings, standings) -> Option<String>`: stale iff (a) a declared dependency has no binding entry, or (b) the binding names a commit and the standing approval names a commit that does not contain it. Not stale when the binding is `None`, and not stale when the dependency has no standing approval (D-068).
   - `HandoffRecord` gains `#[serde(default)] pub dependency_bindings: Vec<DependencyBinding>`; `staleness`/`is_current_for` take a third parameter and now check three of Section 15.2's seven triggers, with the four unchecked ones named in the docstring instead of the old docstring that narrowed the spec to what was implemented.

   - `pub(crate) fn ancestry(scope, ancestor, descendant) -> Result<Option<bool>>` — `None` when Git lacks either object, because the two callers want opposite defaults there.
   - `fn resolve_dependency_bindings(control, scope, depends_on, candidate_sha)` — sorted, deduped, newest-handoff-first ancestry search.

No new error code is introduced at all; `CH-POLICY-DEPENDENCY-EVIDENCE-STALE` and the `ALL` 78→79 plumbing are dropped. The implicit path gets its own test.

2. SILENT SCOPE REDUCTION BECOMES ROUTINE. **Correct, and it was the one hazard nothing in the proposal touched.** `select`'s drop-the-blocked branch stays (refusing there would make the ordinary case — a cycle holding unfinished work — an error; that is the over-correction on this axis). What changed is that the plan now carries what it dropped: `Plan.deferred`, one `warnings` entry per card naming it and why, on both `prepare` and `--dry-run`, plus `deferred` in the preview payload (D-069). Guarded by `a_prepare_that_takes_everything_ready_names_what_it_left_out`, which mutation M4 fails with `the plan must say which cards it left out: []`. Note that under the new rule this path is also much rarer than under the rejected one: only a card that actually incorporates a rewritten dependency commit is dropped.

3. G3 IS VACUOUS AND THE FIX REINSTATES SERIALIZATION. **Correct against the rejected rule, and it is why I changed the rule.** Under incorporated-binding a dependent that branched from the cycle baseline binds `incorporated_sha: null` and can never be invalidated by its dependency, however often it is re-reviewed. G3 is therefore not vacuous, and I added a stronger sibling: `a_dependency_rewrite_does_not_invalidate_a_dependent_that_does_not_incorporate_it` (F-002 declares F-001, branched from baseline, F-001 amended and re-approved — F-002 stays current and both still prepare). Proof the serialization is gone: **no fixture repair was needed.** `tests/integration_plan.rs:158/186` still call `approve_card("F-002")` before `approve_card("F-001")` and both pass untouched — the very order the rejected fix could not tolerate. And for a dependent that *does* incorporate its dependency, D-068 keeps it valid while the dependency is unreviewed, so it does not die the instant the dependency is first approved either.

4. THE SCHEMA CHANGE BREAKS EVERY RECORD FOR NO BENEFIT. **Correct; adopted your precedent.** `#[serde(default)]` on both `HandoffRecord.dependency_bindings` and `ReviewRecord.dependency_bindings`, exactly as `human_reviewer` at src/domain/review.rs:181. `HANDOFF_SCHEMA` and `REVIEW_SCHEMA` are untouched — you are right that nothing reads them, so bumping was cosmetic. No record is rewritten and no regeneration is asked for. The residual: a legacy record for a card that *declares* a dependency reads as "declares one, binds nothing" and is treated as stale. I chose loud over silent there because silently reading it as "no dependencies" is the defect itself; the remedy is a new handoff, which adds a record rather than rewriting one, and it is stated at `dependency_staleness` and in the register.

5. THE RESOLUTION RULE IS NOT THE SPEC'S. **Half accepted.** You are right about the *content* question — the harm is a dependent carrying a superseded dependency commit into the merge alongside its replacement, and that is now the stated rationale and precisely what the check detects. I did not adopt `base_sha` as the mechanism, for three reasons: Section 10.7 requires the handoff's dependency SHAs to be **machine-computed**, and a copy of a declared field is not; ancestry *subsumes* a correct `base_sha` (a card branched at the dependency's accepted commit binds that commit, because it is an ancestor) while also catching a dependent that merged its dependency rather than branching from it; and it does not trust the declaration. Your "record asserts a relationship the reviewer never saw" complaint is answered directly: a dependent whose `base_sha` is the cycle baseline records `incorporated_sha: null`, which is a true statement that it holds nothing of the dependency, and that case is a named test. On the activation-time check at src/policy/allocation.rs:135-167 — I looked, and it cannot carry this: at `card activate` a dependency is usually not yet approved (`activate_card_depending_on` is the normal case), so a declared-base-vs-accepted-dependency check there either passes vacuously or serializes activation behind review. Recorded as considered and rejected rather than silently skipped.

6. `resolve_dependencies` HAS A HOLE (rfind past a later `changes_requested`). **Correct; fixed.** The lookup is now `ReviewRecord::standing_approval` — `reviews.last().filter(approved)`, the standing verdict rather than the last approval anywhere in the chain. Because it is a pure function over a slice it has a unit test that a mutation can fail (M5), which the command-layer version could not have had cheaply.

design.residual_tradeoffs:
1. **A dependency commit that was never handed off cannot be bound.** A dependent branched from a mid-branch commit of its dependency binds `null` and this check says nothing about it, even if that commit is later rewritten away. Stated at `DependencyBinding` and in the register. Closing it would mean walking the dependency's branch history, which is not recorded evidence and disappears when the branch does.

2. **A dependency with no standing approval does not invalidate its dependents** (D-068). A dependent carrying code its dependency's reviewer has since rejected keeps a current approval until the dependency is re-approved somewhere that does not contain it. The cover is that `check_dependencies` refuses any selection whose dependency is neither included nor landed, and an unapproved dependency can be neither — so nothing reaches the authority. The cost is a window where `review inspect` reports an approval that a strict reading of 7.3.6 would void. The alternative voids evidence for the whole time a dependency is under review, which is the parallelism the harness exists for.

3. **An unreachable object is read as "not superseded."** If Git no longer has the dependency's approved candidate, `ancestry` returns `None` and `dependency_standings` defaults to *contained*. The check catches a rewrite it can see rather than demanding proof of innocence. The opposite default would void dependents whenever an unrelated card's branch was archived and collected.

4. **A legacy record that declares a dependency and binds nothing is stale.** `handoff inspect` reports it, integration refuses it, and the remedy is `handoff create` again. Real cost for the self-hosted control repository; chosen over a silent pass.

5. **`handoff create` does not refuse a candidate whose binding is already superseded.** It records the true binding, and the record is born stale. A reviewer can still be asked for a verdict; integration refuses. I did not add a refusal at creation because refusing there is heavy and the information is already reported.

6. **Cost.** `assess` and `review inspect` now run `cat-file -t` and `merge-base --is-ancestor` per declared dependency per review. Zero extra Git calls for a card with no `depends_on`.

7. **Not fixed, recorded instead:** (a) `src/commands/handoff.rs` still writes `baseline_sha: cycle.baseline_sha.unwrap_or(baseline)`, discarding the derived base that `commits`/`changed_paths` were diffed from; (b) `tests/integration_plan.rs::dependencies_are_merged_before_their_dependents` does not test what its name says — the dependency sorts first by identifier anyway. Both are in the register; both are separate defects and folding them in would have muddied this diff.

8. **Section 16.2 still has no scenario for invariant 7.3.6.** Adding a 41st scenario and a trace row is a plan revision with its own procedure (increment revision, update release gates), which I did not perform. The gap is written down.

design.overcorrection_guards:
The opposite failure has three distinct shapes here, and each has a test that fails when a fix takes that shape.

A. **Binding to where the dependency is now rather than to what the candidate holds** — the rejected fix, and the most likely wrong answer, because "which commit is the dependency at" reads as "what is on main". A too-aggressive version voids every dependent the moment its dependency is landed or re-reviewed; no multi-card cycle could then land in two batches, and the parallelism the harness exists for is gone. Guard: `landing_a_dependency_does_not_invalidate_its_dependent` — F-001 goes all the way through merge, land, verify, integration review, acceptance and promotion, the fixture asserts the authority actually moved, and F-002 (lease still held, per your point about `current_approval` being gated on `held_lease`) must still be current and still be the sole entry in `integration ready`. Mutation M6 fails it at :273. Second guard on the same axis: `a_dependency_rewrite_does_not_invalidate_a_dependent_that_does_not_incorporate_it`, failed by M3.

B. **Comparing the bound and approved SHAs for equality instead of containment** — one character of difference, and it makes every ordinary review-and-fix round on a dependency void every dependent that built on it. Guard: `a_dependency_that_only_gained_commits_does_not_invalidate_its_dependent`, with a fixture assertion that the rework really did extend rather than rewrite history. Failed by M2 and again by M6 at :150.

C. **Refusing at the wrong stage.** Two sub-cases. Refusing `handoff create` when a dependency is unapproved would forbid a dependent from ever reaching handoff until its dependency finished — guard `a_dependent_may_be_handed_off_before_its_dependency_is_approved`, which requires exit 0 and a recorded `incorporated_sha: null`. Refusing `review record` would leave a card whose only exit is abandonment, which is defect 20/21 again — that site passes `DEPENDENCIES_NOT_CHECKED`, and the whole existing `tests/review.rs` (20 tests, green) is the standing guard.

D. **Refusing every card in a batch the coordinator did not name** — the over-correction available on objection 2. Not taken: `select` still drops rather than refuses, because a cycle almost always holds unfinished work and refusing would make the common case an error. `tests/integration_plan.rs::omitting_card_ids_selects_every_ready_card` is the guard holding that open, and it is green.

And the opposite of the opposite — a fix that refuses nothing, recording `dependency_bindings` while no staleness path reads them, which satisfies Section 10.7 and leaves 7.3.6 exactly as unimplemented. Mutation M1 is that fix, and it fails the failing-first test **at `has_current_approval`** (:85), not at the error code — confirming the invalidation lives in the record's staleness and not only in an integration-time refusal.

design.design:
The rejected fix's shape was wrong, not just its details. It tried to disable configuration key by key. I replaced it with a porcelain/plumbing split that removes the whole class, then named the two things that genuinely survive the split. Implemented and gated in the worktree at /Users/alvaro/Documents/Code/change-harness/.claude/worktrees/wf_ea9ed2ee-ced-2.

1. `src/git/integration_worktree.rs` — `merge` rewritten.
   `git merge --no-ff --no-commit --no-autostash <candidate>` does the part that is the project's (merge drivers, checkout filters, conflict detection) and stops before any commit. The harness then authors the object itself: `write-tree` -> `commit-tree <tree> -p <before> -p <MERGE_HEAD> -m <message>` -> `update-ref HEAD <new> <before>` (compare-and-swap) -> `reset -q` (clears MERGE_HEAD/MERGE_MSG; verified the index already matches, so it moves no content).
   Because Git never composes a message and never writes a commit, `commit.gpgsign`, `gpg.*`, `merge.log`, `commit.template`, `commit.cleanup`, `prepare-commit-msg`, `commit-msg`, `pre-merge-commit` and `post-commit` are all out of reach by construction. Nothing enumerates them.
   `--no-autostash` is load-bearing, not tidiness — see objection-5 note below.
   New private helpers: `hook_sink()` (per-invocation `tempfile::TempDir`), `merge_head()`, `verify_authored()`, `run_post_merge_hook()`.

2. `src/git/command.rs` — `run_with_config` / `run_with_config_ok` inject `-c` between the scope prefix and the subcommand; `run` delegates with an empty list so no existing call site changes. `authoring_overrides(hook_sink)` returns exactly two entries, each with its reason written at the definition:
   - `core.hooksPath=<private temp dir>` — the only hook still reachable in the sequence is `reference-transaction`, which fires on `MERGE_HEAD` and on the `update-ref`, and can abort either (verified: exit 128, "ref updates aborted by hook").
   - `merge.verifySignatures=false` — stops `git merge` before content is combined, so it survives everything aimed at the commit.
   `strip_ambient_overrides(&mut Command)` is exposed so the hook the harness runs itself starts from the same sanitised environment as every Git call.

3. `run_post_merge_hook` — Git no longer runs `post-merge`, so the harness runs it: resolve `rev-parse --git-path hooks` (which honours `core.hooksPath`, so a relocated hook dir still works), spawn `<hooks>/post-merge` with argv `["0"]`, cwd at the worktree top, `GIT_DIR` set from `rev-parse --absolute-git-dir`, ambient overrides stripped, exit status ignored. The stated line: **a hook that materialises the working tree keeps running; a hook that authors, vetoes or observes a commit does not.**

4. `verify_authored` — reads the object back and refuses a `gpgsig` header, parents other than `[before, MERGE_HEAD]`, or a body other than the message passed. It compares the **whole message**, not a subject, and runs **before** `update-ref` so a refusal leaves the worktree recoverable by the caller's `abort_merge`.

5. Classification. On the non-zero-exit branch only: `MERGE_HEAD` present -> `ConflictMergeFailed` ("did not apply"); absent -> new `ErrorCode::PreconditionMergeRefused` / `CH-PRECONDITION-MERGE-REFUSED`, exit 4. `src/error.rs`: `ALL` 78 -> 79, plus the category, detail and remediation arms. The remediation names no cause — it points at Git's own diagnostic and says nothing was combined, explicitly not `integration preflight`.

6. `src/control/repository.rs` — `initialize_git` now runs `git -C <root> -c init.templateDir= init -q -b main`, and writes `commit.gpgsign=false` and `core.hooksPath=<root>/.git/change-harness-no-hooks` into the control repo's own local config. Local beats `~/.gitconfig`. This is the opposite treatment from the candidate repo and deliberately so: the control repo is created and written only by the harness, so declaring it hook-free and signature-free in its own config is not "fixing the operator's machine".

7. `src/commands/integration.rs` — `synchronize_local_main` unchanged; a paragraph at the call site states why: `--ff-only` writes no commit, so nothing there is a harness-authored object, and `post-merge` on the developer's own protected worktree is the project finishing its checkout. Verified it cannot block. The finding's part D asked for neutrality "or a stated reason"; I chose the reason.

Production sites that create commits, from `grep -rn '"commit"|"merge"|commit-tree|"am"|"cherry-pick"|"rebase"|"tag"|"stash"' src`: `control/repository.rs:346`, `git/landing.rs:118` (`commit-tree`, unaffected), `git/integration_worktree.rs`, `commands/integration.rs:2504` (`--ff-only`, no commit). Everything else the grep returned is a test helper (`archive.rs:173`, `worktree.rs:268`, `backup.rs:327`, `authority.rs:293` are all inside `#[cfg(test)]`). `merge-tree` and `commit-tree` are left alone.
design.answers_each_objection:
**1. `merge.log` is not neutralised, and check B would refuse every integration on a repo that sets it.** Correct and now moot. Git no longer composes the message at all — `commit-tree -m` writes it verbatim. Verified directly (probe q2 section B): with `merge.log = true`, the body is exactly `integrate F-001 into INT-001` with no shortlog, where a porcelain merge appends `* commit '...':`. So check B compares the *whole* message rather than a subject, and it cannot over-refuse, because there is nothing left that can append to it. The test `an_integration_merge_carries_the_harness_message_whatever_the_project_configures` sets `merge.log = true` **and** installs a hijacking `prepare-commit-msg` in the same fixture, precisely so a fix that closes one route and not the other fails.

**2. `merge.verifySignatures` still blocks and gets the wrong remediation.** Correct on both counts. Reproduced: exit 128, no `MERGE_HEAD`, zero unmerged entries. Two changes. It is now named explicitly in `authoring_overrides` with its reason (the harness decides what may be integrated from the plan and the review record; D-006/D-013 put candidate provenance outside this tool's trust model) and covered by `a_signature_policy_on_the_repository_does_not_block_an_integration`. And the remediation for the refusal code no longer names `commit.gpgsign`, `core.hooksPath` or "the repository's hooks" — it names Git's own diagnostic, because the set of things that refuse a merge before it starts is open and any list would misdirect for the rest.

**3. `ls-files -u` separates conflicts from *everything else*, not from environment refusals.** Correct, and the discriminator is gone. I classify on `MERGE_HEAD` — Git's own record of "a merge is under way" — not on the index. Verified across five states on git 2.50.1: content conflict = exit 1, MERGE_HEAD set, 3 unmerged; untracked-file-would-be-overwritten = exit 2, no MERGE_HEAD, 0 unmerged; `merge.verifySignatures` = exit 128, no MERGE_HEAD; local-changes-would-be-overwritten = exit 2, no MERGE_HEAD; already-up-to-date = exit 0, no MERGE_HEAD. Your untracked case is exactly the one I built the failing test on, and it lands in the "refused before anything was combined" arm with a diagnostic-first remediation. Note also that this does not claim to identify a *cause* — it claims only "content was combined" vs "content was never combined", which is the distinction the operator actually needs and the only one the evidence supports.

**4. The fix creates the harm its own overcorrection section forbids: `core.hooksPath` kills `post-merge`.** Correct, and this is the objection that changed the design most. Under `--no-commit`, Git runs no commit-stage hook *and* no `post-merge`, so the harness runs `post-merge` itself: `run_post_merge_hook`, with Git's own argv and cwd and `GIT_DIR`. `an_integration_merge_still_runs_the_projects_post_merge_hook` asserts the hook ran and received `squash=0`. Under MUT-A (the whole fix reverted) that test **passes**, which is what proves it is a guard on the new code and not an accidental duplicate; under MUT-B (only the explicit call removed) it fails at `left: "" right: "squash=0"`. The `create` site is untouched for the same reason, and `worktree_creation_still_runs_the_projects_checkout_hooks` holds that line. The residual cost is stated at `create` rather than hidden — see residual trade-offs.

**5 (your "missed" list, item 5). Defect 17's `head == before` guard.** The classifier runs only inside `if !output.success()`. The already-contained case is a separate `let Some(...) else` on the success path and keeps `ConflictMergeFailed`. I added an explicit `assert_eq!(error.code(), ErrorCode::ConflictMergeFailed)` to `merging_a_commit_already_contained_is_refused_rather_than_reported_merged` so the interaction is pinned rather than implied — both arms read the same absent `MERGE_HEAD` and only the exit status separates them.

**6 (item 6). The hook sink was inside a directory the project controls.** Fixed rather than excused: a per-invocation `tempfile::TempDir` with an unpredictable name, created by the harness and removed when `merge` returns. The control repository's sink is a fixed path under its own `.git`, which is fine because the harness owns that repository outright.

**Items 1, 3, 4, 7.** The register entry is updated in place rather than written as a new discovery. The blast radius (landing commit's second parent, so it reaches the protected branch permanently) is now the opening sentence of `merge`'s doc comment. The `run_smoke_gates` reachability is cited in the untracked-file test's comment. The site search is shown above and recorded.

**One place I found you incomplete.** `reference-transaction` is a fourth route neither the finding nor your review names, and it is the one that survives the porcelain/plumbing split: a hook exiting non-zero aborts `update-ref` at exit 128 and also aborts the `MERGE_HEAD` write inside `git merge --no-commit`. It is why `core.hooksPath` is still in the override list at all, and `a_reference_transaction_hook_cannot_block_an_integration_merge` is the only test that can show that flag is carrying weight. The enumeration was incomplete in both directions.
design.residual_tradeoffs:
1. **A refusing `reference-transaction` hook still blocks `integration_worktree::create`.** `git worktree add` writes a ref, and that site deliberately keeps the project's hooks so `post-checkout` still materialises the tree. `core.hooksPath` is all-or-nothing, so there is no way to have one without the other there. Recorded at the `create` doc comment as unfixed, with the reason. It surfaces as `CH-EXTERNAL-GIT-COMMAND` carrying "ref updates aborted by hook", which is at least accurate. The test installs its hook after `create` for exactly this reason, and says so.

2. **`merge.verifySignatures` is now ignored.** An operator who set it to enforce signed candidates loses that enforcement inside the harness's merge. I took this side because the harness's admission decision comes from the plan and the review record, and D-006/D-013 already declare candidate provenance out of scope — but it is a real capability removed, not a no-op.

3. **`post-merge` residue still trips `is_clean`.** Running the hook preserves today's behaviour including its downside: a `post-merge` that writes into the worktree makes `build_integration` fail with "integration worktree is not clean after merging". Not fixed here; suppressing the hook would "fix" it by breaking objection 4's case.

4. **`post-merge` is unbounded in time**, as Git's invocation is. A hanging hook hangs the integration. Unchanged from today, so not a regression, but the harness now owns the call.

5. **`.gitattributes` merge drivers still run** and can execute arbitrary commands. Deliberate — that is the project's merge semantics, and the alternative is producing a tree no developer would get. Verified they still run under `--no-commit`. Same trust level as today.

6. **Exit-status change.** The untracked-residue path now exits 4 (`CH-PRECONDITION-MERGE-REFUSED`) where it exited 6. A caller matching on 6 for "the merge failed" sees a new code. The two existing end-to-end assertions on exit 6 (`tests/merge_preflight.rs:193`, `tests/landing_commit.rs:381`) are genuine content-conflict and tamper paths and still pass.

7. **`verify_authored` refuses with `InternalControlCorrupt`** (exit 10, "report this as a defect"). If a future Git makes `commit-tree` honour `commit.gpgsign`, the operator is told the harness is broken. I think that is right — the premise the design rests on would have broken — but it is a harsh code for an environment change.

8. **`--no-autostash` can refuse where today's merge succeeded**: a smoke gate that modifies a tracked file the next candidate also touches, with `merge.autoStash = true` set. Verified: exit 2, no MERGE_HEAD, so it reports as a refusal with Git's own "Your local changes would be overwritten". I took this side because the alternative silently moves the gate's work into a stash entry and makes `is_clean` lie.

9. **No end-to-end test of the new error code through the CLI envelope.** The classifier is covered at the unit level only; a full-lifecycle fixture that plants residue between merges was more machinery than the finding justifies.

1. THE CONTRACT IS A CONVENTION, NOT A TYPE. Nothing in the type system stops a future `cycle.*` event type from being wrong, or a non-`cycle.*` event from claiming a cycle transition. What stands behind it is a doc'd const, seven unit tests pinning today's shapes, one end-to-end tripwire, and a runtime warning. A command that moved the cycle in a path `tests/lifecycle.rs` never exercises would only surface at runtime, as a warning a human has to read. I considered a source-scanning test over `EventDraft::new("...")` literals and rejected it: it would not have caught M7 (no new event type there), so it would buy brittleness without buying the property.

2. THE DERIVED STATUS CAN NOW ONLY EVER BE draft/active/abandoned. This fix does not create that — it stops card noise from disguising it. `tests/lifecycle.rs` now ASSERTS `"active"` after a fully promoted, archived, closed lifecycle. That bakes a known incompleteness into a test, on purpose, with the reason written above the assertion. Whoever closes the "five unreachable cycle statuses" item will fail it and must emit `cycle.*` events. The cost: an assertion that reads like it endorses a defect.

3. `card.created` STILL RENDERS `-`. The subject genuinely is not in the event. `-` is honest; it is also uglier than an id and a reader has to know what it means (the doc comment says). Fixing it properly means `card.created` setting `.card(..)`, which is a separate change and cannot relabel events already written.

5. `audit cycle` STILL TRUSTS THE STORED FIELD. The two commands agree today only because nothing outside cycle.rs writes a cycle status. My cross-command test would go red on a real tamper, which is arguably the wrong reason for it to fail — it is a coherence check, not a correctness check for either side.

6. THE FIX IS AT THE CALL SITE, NOT THE STORE. `derived_status` and `run_status` each filter independently. A third caller wanting "the cycle's own transitions" must remember to filter. The alternative — a `for_cycle_transitions` method — would have tempted someone to narrow `for_cycle` and break the audit timeline, which verifier-missed #2 warns about.

**1. The event fold — `src/domain/cycle.rs`, `src/commands/cycle.rs`.**

design.answers_each_objection:
**Objection 1 — `card abandon` as specified refuses the scenario that motivates it. CORRECT, and decisive.** Reproduced twice. First independently: a card with one ordinary commit on `card/F-001`, then `rev-list refs/heads/card/F-001 --not <every other ref>` returns exactly one commit, so `clean_up_card`'s first check fires. Then as mutation M6, by wiring the rejected design's `unarchived_commits` precondition into my `card abandon` and running the suite: `abandoning_a_card_destroys_neither_its_branch_nor_its_worktree` fails with `CH-PRECONDITION-UNMERGED-WORK`, "branch `card/F-001` holds 1 commit(s) reachable from nowhere else; archive them before cleanup". The verifier is right that this is unfixable as designed and right that overcorrection guard 4 pins the hole open. My design removes the cleanup coupling entirely.

**Objection 2 — the cleanup coupling is unnecessary; transition always, cleanup opt-in or best-effort. CORRECT, and I take the strictest reading of it.** `Claim::holds_claims` (src/policy/allocation.rs:59) reads `CardState` alone, so the transition by itself frees the region — which is the motivating outcome. I chose neither opt-in nor best-effort: `card abandon` does zero Git. Opt-in re-arms the trap whenever the flag is passed (the transaction is atomic, so the refusal would take the transition down with it), and best-effort makes the command's behaviour depend on Git state and needs an `outside_control` boundary for a mutation nobody asked for. Doing nothing is smaller, has no failure modes, and is honest — the outcome names the branch it left behind.

**Objection 3 — "no command able to release it" is false; `card revise` is an escape. CORRECT, and I verified it.** Real run: F-001 `blocked` holding `src/shared/**`; F-002 refused `CH-POLICY-OWNERSHIP-OVERLAP`; `card revise --card-id F-001` narrowing to `src/dead-end/**` exits 0 and lands in `ready`; F-002 then activates, exit 0. So the severity was overstated. **But I also found what the verifier did not:** after that escape, `git worktree list` still shows `worktrees/F-001` locked and allocated to F-001, on branch `card/F-001`. The escape releases the write scope and leaves the lease, worktree and branch behind, and it does so by falsifying the card's definition — the record now claims a scope the work never touched, in the audit trail the product exists to produce. That is a worse artefact than an honest `abandoned`. The defect is real and worth fixing; only its stated severity was wrong, and I have not restated it.

**Objection 4 — `cycle block` and `cycle close` would be decorative; the proposal says the opposite. CORRECT, and worse than stated.** `grep -rn "accepts_cards\|cycle\.status" src` gives four hits outside `src/domain/cycle.rs`: `card.rs:290` (the only enforcement), `integration.rs:415` and `:462` (both report-only in `integration ready`), `audit.rs:242`/`:288` (report). I then proved the live consequence end to end: activate C-001, approve F-001, `cycle abandon`, then `integration prepare` → exit 0, and merge, land, verify, review, acceptance, promote all succeed — the authority branch moved for an abandoned cycle. So the hole is not hypothetical for a future `cycle close`; it is open today for `cycle abandon`. My answer has two halves: I do not build the decorative commands (so the objection does not apply to my design), and I close the live half with the `integration prepare` refusal (D-057), which is precisely the verifier's own missed item 4.

**Objection 5 — deleting three specified states rests on a contestable reading presented as settled. CORRECT.** Two integrations per cycle is an unchecked behaviour, not a recorded decision; Section 11.1 is the written specification; the glossary says "a bounded integration period", singular; and removing variants narrows what `harness.cycle/v1` deserializes with no schema bump in a repo that versions records deliberately. The symmetric repair — refuse `integration prepare` once an integration has archived, and wire integrating/accepted/landed — was never weighed. I do not delete anything. D-058 records both candidates, names the unmade decision, and marks it Open.

**Objection 6 — compound trap: a cycle holding one given-up card with committed work can never close. CORRECT, and dissolved rather than answered.** It was the product of objections 1 and the proposed `cycle close` precondition. With no cleanup coupling and no `cycle close`, the trap has no components left. Should `cycle close` be built later, the card-terminality precondition is now satisfiable, because `card abandon` reaches `abandoned` from every non-landed state with no Git precondition.

**Verifier-missed 1 — `card revise` performs an unchecked transition.** Confirmed live: `Blocked -> Ready` exits 0 and is not in Section 11.2. `run_revise` guards with `is_revisable` (defect 19's fix) and never restored `check_transition`. Real and unfixed — a distinct defect in a distinct function, out of this key's scope. Flagged, not smuggled in.

**Verifier-missed 2 — `audit.rs` reads the stored status, so fixing the fold leaves the report saying `active` forever. WRONG, and I proved it.** `audit.rs:242` reads `cycle.status`, the record's own field, which every cycle command writes alongside its own event. Probe: create, activate, abandon C-001, then `audit cycle --cycle-id C-001` → `"status": "abandoned"`, and `cycle status` → `"abandoned"`. The two agree; they diverge only under external tampering, which `cycle status` surfaces as a warning by design. Before my fix the *derived* value was the wrong one and the stored one was right, so the fold fix moves audit toward agreement rather than away from it. No change needed.

**Verifier-missed 3 — `archive create` is integration-scoped, so an abandoned card's commits cannot be preserved. CORRECT, and it is the load-bearing fact.** It is exactly why cleanup cannot be coupled to the transition, and it is written at the check in `run_abandon`'s doc comment and in D-056 as the work a future card-scoped archive ref must do.

**Verifier-missed 4 — nothing refuses `integration prepare` or `promote` on a terminal cycle. CORRECT.** Implemented for `prepare` only. `promote` is deliberately left permissive, and mutation M8 shows why: adding the same check there fails `an_integration_already_open_when_the_cycle_is_abandoned_still_archives` — an integration open when the cycle was abandoned could never reach `archive close`, which is what releases its members' worktrees and branches. Planning is refused; finishing is not.

**Verifier-missed 5 — the register already records both halves as open. CORRECT.** `docs/DEFECT-REGISTER.md` Tier 4 says verbatim "Cycle status folds card events. Five cycle statuses and one card state are unreachable." I have edited that sentence in place rather than presenting anything as fresh.

**Verifier-missed 6 — `existing_claims` iterates `cycle.card_ids`, populated only at `card activate`. CORRECT and now moot**, since I build no `cycle close` precondition over `card_ids`.

**"What does hold up" — the `"cycle."` prefix filter breaks nothing (801 tests, zero failures).** Reproduced: 819 passing, zero failures, and no existing fixture asserted the contaminated fold.
design.residual_tradeoffs:
**1. `card abandon` leaves debris, permanently.** The branch `card/<id>` and the worktree survive, and nothing in the harness reclaims them. Abandon fifty cards and you have fifty locked worktrees and fifty branches. This is a deliberate trade — disk and namespace against destroying an operator's only copy of a commit — and it stays until a card-scoped archive ref exists so the branch has somewhere safe to go. Recorded at `run_abandon`'s doc comment and in D-056, and held open by `abandoning_a_card_destroys_neither_its_branch_nor_its_worktree`.

**2. The stale lease is not released either.** The abandoned card's `held_lease` record still points at the retained worktree. Nothing reads it for an abandoned card (`work start` requires `ready`), so it is inert — but it is a control record describing something the model considers finished, and I have not audited every reader of `held_lease` to prove that inertness for all time.

**3. Five cycle statuses stay unreachable.** `integrating`, `accepted`, `landed`, `closed`, `blocked` still have no writer. A coordinator who *finishes* a cycle has no way to say so; the only ending remains `abandoned`, which is a false entry in the audit trail for a cycle that landed everything. This is the single biggest thing I am not fixing, and it is the honest cost of not making the one-vs-many-integrations decision.

**4. `integration prepare` is the only enforcement point.** A cycle abandoned mid-flight can still merge, land, verify, review, accept, promote and archive its existing integration, and the authority branch will move. I argue that is correct (the alternative strands the integration's worktrees — mutation M8), but it is a real hole in "abandoning a cycle stops work", and the line is drawn at planning by judgement, not by anything the specification says.

**5. The fold filter is a string prefix.** If a future command emits a `cycle.`-prefixed event that is not a cycle transition, it will be folded; if a cycle command emits a differently-named event, it will be dropped. `cycle_event_types_come_only_from_cycle_commands` states the convention but cannot enforce it against source it does not scan.

**6. `check_abandonable` scans every integration record for the cycle on each call.** Linear in integrations, same as `build_plan` and `integration ready` already are. Not a problem at any plausible scale, and consistent with the existing shape.

**7. `card revise`'s unchecked transition is left in place.** Confirmed live (`blocked -> ready`, exit 0, not in Section 11.2). It is a separate defect in a separate function and fixing it here would widen the blast radius of a fix that has already been rejected once.

design.overcorrection_guards:
Five opposite failures, each named and each held open by a test with a mutation behind it.

**1. `card abandon` too destructive.** A version that removes the worktree and deletes the branch destroys uncommitted work and commits reachable from nowhere else. Guard: T9 `abandoning_a_card_destroys_neither_its_branch_nor_its_worktree`, which leaves both a real commit and an uncommitted file and asserts all three survive (branch ref, commit object via `cat-file -e`, file on disk). Mutation M6 — the rejected design's own precondition — fails it with `CH-PRECONDITION-UNMERGED-WORK`.

**2. `card abandon` too refusing.** Coupling cleanup to the transition refuses exactly the case the command exists for, because a card that never reached an integration always has unarchived commits. This is objection 1, and it is the same case as guard 1: the rejected proposal made the refusal a *required* test and so pinned the hole open. My design has no Git precondition at all, and T8 proves the ordinary give-up path (worked, blocked, committed) succeeds and frees the region.

**3. `card abandon` too permissive.** Abandoning a member of a live integration wedges it: the plan pins a terminal card and `accepted -> landed` can never fire. Guard: T10, whose mutation M5 lands on the refusal assertion with `left: Some(0)`, proving `check_transition` alone permits it. And T10's tail runs `integration abandon` and then abandons the card successfully, so the guard cannot be satisfied by a refusal with no way out.

**4. Cycle enforcement too broad.** Refusing every integration step on a terminal cycle strands an in-flight integration — `archive close` is what releases its members' worktrees and branches, so a cycle abandoned after promotion could never be cleaned up. Guard: T7 `an_integration_already_open_when_the_cycle_is_abandoned_still_archives`, which prepares first, abandons second, and drives all the way to `archive close` asserting F-001 reaches `closed`. Mutation M8 (the same check at `promote`) fails it with `cycle C-001 is 'abandoned' and cannot promote`.

**5. The event filter too broad or too narrow.** Too narrow — `card_id.is_none()` — still folds `acceptance.recorded`; mutation M2′ proves it, failing T3 precisely at `acceptance record`. Too broad — drop the fold and trust the stored field — discards `WP-200`'s "history is authoritative" and makes T5 vacuous; T5 now tampers a genuinely-abandoned cycle and requires the derived value to win, and mutation M3 (constant fold) fails it on that exact assertion.

**6. Too much removal, pre-empted.** Deleting `Closed` would leave `abandoned` as a cycle's only ending, a false entry in the audit trail for a cycle that landed everything. I delete nothing, so the guard is unnecessary — but the failure is real and named in D-058 as a cost of the deletion candidate, which is why I did not take it.
